extracted.subtask_description: Principles and observational criteria for deciding when a mammalian character (colour, hair, odour, or other secondary sexual trait) is best explained by sexual selection rather than by natural selection or by simple variability. Includes behavioral, developmental, anatomical, and comparative lines of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of specialised odour glands as evidence of sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The odour emitted must be of considerable importance to the male, inasmuch as large and complex glands, furnished with muscles for everting the sack, and for closing or opening the orifice, have in some cases been developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If males possess well-developed, often muscular scent-glands and are more odoriferous than females, this supports the view that odour functions in sexual selection (i.e. attracts or excites mates or aids rivalry). Reject simpler explanations such as general attraction from a distance when other evidence contradicts this. Examples: dogs and carrion-sniffing, males with stronger odours; caution that odour might serve other functions in some taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusually developed hair/skins in males (crests, manes, dewlaps) suggest ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Male quadrupeds often have hair on their necks and shoulders much more developed than the females (manes, crests, throat brushes, dewlaps), sometimes in places unlikely to afford protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such appendages are unlikely to serve protective or utilitarian purposes (e.g., a thin crest along the back that affords little defence), their presence restricted to or exaggerated in males points toward sexual selection as an origin (ornamental or for rival display). But consider alternative explanations: simple sexually-limited variability or artificial selection in domesticates. Example taxa: Tragelaphus scriptus, Portax picta, Pithecia, Ammotragus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of trait upon emasculation indicates sexual (hormonal) origin
rubrics_metrics.description: A true secondary sexual character is not developed if the animal be castrated; emasculation causes loss or non-development of many male-specific characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trait appears only in intact males and is lost or fails to develop after castration, this is strong evidence it is sexually produced (hormonally mediated) and thus likely the result of sexual selection rather than being an ordinary variant. Examples: mane in certain rams and seasonal colour changes prevented by emasculation (Portax, Banteng).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance at or near sexual maturity supports sexual_selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Such colours and ornaments do not appear in the male at birth, but only at or near maturity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits that develop at the age when the animal becomes reproductive are more plausibly explained as secondary sexual characters acquired by sexual selection. Contrast with traits present at birth which may be ancestral or serve other functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal development (breeding coat) as indicator of sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of colour is sometimes seasonal, and the tints of the naked parts sometimes become more vivid during the act of courtship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If bright colours or ornaments intensify during breeding season or appear in a breeding coat, this timing supports a sexual-selection function. Examples: Portax pica darkening in breeding season, Virginian deer breeding coat changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male-biased vividness and ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: In both classes the male is almost always more vividly or strongly coloured than the female, and is ornamented with larger crests of hair or feathers, or other such appendages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A consistent pattern of males being more brightly coloured or ornamented than females across related taxa is evidence that sexual selection has acted on males. Note exceptions exist (females sometimes more ornamented). Use comparative context across groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation with other secondary sexual characters
rubrics_metrics.description: These colours and other ornamental characters occur almost exclusively in those groups and sub-groups of mammals which present other and strongly-marked secondary sexual characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When bright colours/ornaments co-occur with other male secondary sexual traits (weapons, larger canines, stronger voice), this concordance strengthens the sexual-selection explanation. Look for clusters of sexually dimorphic traits in taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous/singular colours unlikely for protection argue sexual origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Although many quadrupeds have received their present tints either as a protection, or as an aid in procuring prey, yet with a host of species, the colours are far too conspicuous and too singularly arranged to allow us to suppose that they serve for these purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If coloration is highly conspicuous or oddly patterned in ways that do not aid concealment or hunting, it is improbable to be an adaptation for protection and is more likely due to sexual selection (ornamentation). Examples: brightly patterned antelopes (Damalis), mandrill facial colours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral responsiveness to colour as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Quadrupeds manifestly take notice of colour (e.g., a female zebra refused a male ass until painted to resemble a zebra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct behavioral observations showing animals prefer or respond to colour/patterns support the hypothesis that such traits are used in mate choice or species recognition. Look for experiments, keeper observations, or field reports indicating stimulus value of colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission of male-acquired ornaments to both sexes
rubrics_metrics.description: With many birds, ornaments, which analogy leads us to believe were primarily acquired by the males, have been transmitted equally, or almost equally, to both sexes; the same may apply to mammals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an ornament is present in both sexes, consider a history where it was first acquired by males and later partly transmitted to females (genetic correlation), or alternatively that it serves protective purposes in both sexes. Examine comparative distribution and functional arguments to distinguish these possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juvenile resemblance and ancestral retention (not sexual selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: When young animals follow nearly the same habits of life as their parents, and yet are coloured in a different manner, it may be inferred that they have retained the colouring of some ancient and extinct progenitor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If juveniles show markings (e.g., spots or stripes) that adults lack, interpret these as possible ancestral retention rather than recent sexual selection; use ontogenetic series and comparative phylogenetic context (e.g., fawns spotted, adults not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Camouflage/seasonal whiteness indicates natural selection for protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Quadrupeds inhabiting snow-clad regions have been rendered white to protect them from their enemies, or to favour their stealing on their prey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coloration clearly matches background environments (seasonal whitening, snow camouflage), natural selection for concealment is a plausible cause. Distinguish these adaptive cases from ornamentation by examining environment, seasonality, and fitness consequences.
